roundReason: Architect's standing ruling (PR comments 6400492408, 6400601649, 6400670216, 6400709005): cleanup() ignores further INT/TERM/HUP; the hazard sentences come out. The implementer added 'trap '' INT TERM HUP; set -m' (set -m because kubectl does not keep an ignored SIGTERM).

implementerProof.how: Its TERM cases reproduce: two TERMs 0.5 s apart (infra-386-postgres-gspgq) and one TERM into a failed run's trap (b84xv) each finished and printed sequence: exit; the ignore without set -m printed 'cleanup: the Job's delete failed' and left the Job, Service and pod (sdwjw); SIGKILL left them (zlgnj) and the recovery lines removed them in 5.8 s; a plain run ended exit 0 with nothing left. But it drove only SIGTERM as the stop, and the page's claim covers SIGINT and SIGHUP too. SIGINT reaching the trap still kills it (failure below), so the proof does not establish the claim it is cited for.

failures.criterion: The page's claim at docs/kubernetes.md:3211-3216 of 90eca150: 'Once the trap runs, it ignores further SIGINT, SIGTERM and SIGHUP ... a stop sent to the sequence's group while the trap runs — a second stop, or one sent after a failed step or the work's end started the trap — reaches neither the trap nor its commands, and the clean-up runs to its end', and the closing comment that now lists only SIGKILL/pod loss, a failed clean-up step and the late-stored create as ways to leave the workload (the architect's ruling: 'no stop of any kind, from any start, cuts a clean-up short')
failures.evidence: A SIGINT that reaches the sequence while its trap runs still ends the trap part-way, with no 'sequence: exit' line, and leaves the Job, its Service and its pod. Reproduced on the real block at the head, filled in, from this issue's role container against the applied cluster, with drive.sh SCRIPT OUT WAITFOR SIG@delay...: starts the filled block (the page's own flock ... setsid -f lines), waits until the sequence's own log matches WAITFOR, then sends each signal to the sequence's process group (kill -SIG -- -<process>) or, as bash:SIG, to its bash alone; run with TMPDIR set to a private directory: (1) work fixture 'sleep 120', kill -TERM -- -<process> once it answered, kill -INT -- -<process> 0.3 s later: 5 of 5 runs (infra-386-postgres-jgczj, mtfmz, tt9kt, qt7df, and the storm run rzxxw) printed 'Terminated' and the first readings, then nothing; Job, Service and pod still there 3 s after the sequence ended. (2) A single stop: work fixture 'false', one kill -INT -- -<process> as the trap's readings began (db4zr): nothing after the readings' first line, Job, Service and pod left. (3) SIGINT to the bash alone: TERM to the group then INT to the bash 0.3 s later (4zc4h) left all three; at 1.2 s (g9bjx) no 'sequence: exit' line (the delete had been sent, so nothing was left). Controls at the same head: TERM then TERM (c8cdf), TERM then HUP (8mhz2) and the TERM-only cases above each printed 'sequence: exit 143' or 'sequence: exit 1' and left nothing; and the same block without 'set -m' (t7-sleep-nom.sh) ignored a SIGINT to its bash and printed 'sequence: exit 143' (d6m5n). So 'set -m' is what makes SIGINT kill the trap's bash; putting 'set -m' before the 'trap '' …' (t7-sleep-swap.sh) did not help (2 of 2 runs, 2rqqc and 47fr8, left all three). Every leftover was removed with the page's two name-based recovery lines. No red test: the block lives in prose, no suite runs it, and the deployment instructions bar tests that assert a file's contents; the drive.sh commands above are the reproduction.
